papers.contribution: A hierarchical back-end for neural implicit SLAM with two necessary co-contributions: residual-conditioned initialization of multiresolution submaps followed by joint local map/trajectory optimization, and hierarchical feature-space alignment plus feature-space fusion across submaps for global consistency. Pretrained encoders and a shared decoder support the local stage; final SDF-based alignment refines the feature-based global stage. The paper presents both local acceleration and global submap optimization, not just a new scene representation.

evidence.statement: MISO represents a scene as posed multiresolution feature-grid submaps. Its back-end addresses local SLAM within submaps and global alignment/fusion between submaps, using odometry and point clouds from depth images or LiDAR.
evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III (Overview) and Section IV-A; p. 12, Section VIII (Conclusion).

evidence.statement: Encoders and decoder are pretrained offline and fixed during the proposed local optimization; online variables are grid features and robot poses. Replica-pretrained weights are used on ScanNet and FastCaMo-Large without additional fine-tuning.
evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Sections III and IV-A; p. 7, Section VI-A; p. 13, Appendix A.

evidence.statement: With a linear decoder and quadratic costs, the optimal level's initialization is a linear function of residuals left by coarser levels. For nonlinear decoding, separate learned encoders map those residuals to progressively finer feature grids; all grid levels and robot poses are then jointly optimized.
evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section IV-B; p. 5, Proposition 1, equations (8)-(11), and Algorithm 1; p. 14, proof.

evidence.statement: Global alignment updates submap base poses by minimizing discrepancies between overlapping interpolated feature fields at transformed query coordinates. Levels are included from coarse to fine. These feature-based iterations avoid decoding SDF values and do not require explicit geometric correspondences.
evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section V, equations (16)-(17) and Algorithm 2; p. 7, opening paragraph; p. 9, alignment discussion.

evidence.statement: A final SDF-disagreement stage refines submap poses. In Table VI, ScanNet 0011 from 10-degree/0.25-m initial errors, coarse-plus-fine features give 3.68 degrees/0.12 m in 2.54 s; adding SDF refinement gives 2.71 degrees/0.09 m in 10.13 s, averaged over ten trials.
evidence.location: PDF p. 7, equations (18)-(19); p. 11, Section VI-E and Table VI, scene 0011.

evidence.statement: For a world-frame query, fusion transforms the query into covering submaps, averages their interpolated implicit features using bounding-box membership weights, and decodes that average. It does not average independently decoded SDF values or merge explicit meshes as its fusion rule.
evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section V (Submap Fusion), equations (20)-(21).

evidence.statement: On ScanNet 0011, with 5-degree/0.20-m initial submap errors, MISO reports 10.53 s GPU time and final errors 1.86 degrees/0.06 m; MIPS reports 59.23 s and 3.93 degrees/0.15 m, and VFPP 74.16 s and 2.40 degrees/0.11 m. Results average ten trials; neural methods use 100 alignment iterations.
evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table III and Section VI-B (Submap alignment and fusion evaluation).

evidence.statement: On ScanNet 0011 with ground-truth poses, MISO reports 0.80 s, 6.07-cm Chamfer-L1, and 71.23% F-score; iSDF reports 25.89 s, 6.35 cm, and 67.32%. F-score uses a 5-cm threshold. MISO runs 20 online epochs versus 100 for iSDF, which lacks the pretraining.
evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table I and Section VI-B (Local SLAM evaluation).

evidence.statement: Evaluation includes ScanNet, FastCaMo-Large, and outdoor Newer College. The authors identify dense-grid memory scaling and predominantly offline batch evaluation of static scenes as limitations; the incremental extension disables encoder initialization, and its Newer College experiments pretrain a decoder per scene.
evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section IV-C; p. 7, Section VI-A; p. 10, Sections VI-C and VI-D; p. 11, Section VII.

papers.initial_draft: MISO is a neural SLAM back-end that represents an environment with multiresolution submaps. It uses pretrained encoders to initialize finer-level features from residuals left by coarser levels, then optimizes features and robot poses together. A second stage aligns submaps using their features and applies SDF refinement before fusion. The method was tested on ScanNet, FastCaMo-Large, and Newer College. On ScanNet scene 0011, alignment took 10.53 seconds versus 59.23 seconds for MIPS, starting with errors of 5 degrees and 0.20 meters. The results show faster optimization with competitive accuracy. Dense grids can require substantial memory in larger environments.

relations.meaning: Local information flows from a coarser prediction's remaining measurement residuals into the encoder for a finer feature grid. Learned initialization precedes, rather than replaces, joint optimization of map features and robot poses.
relations.original_witness: It uses pretrained encoders to initialize finer-level features from residuals left by coarser levels, then optimizes features and robot poses together.

relations.meaning: The global operations act on the implicit features: alignment compares overlapping feature fields to update submap poses, and fusion averages aligned features before decoding a global prediction. Avoiding repeated SDF decoding applies to feature-alignment iterations, not to the final SDF refinement or decoded fused output.

questions.question: What information initializes each finer feature level, and what is still optimized after initialization?
questions.answer: Residuals left by coarser predictions initialize finer features through pretrained encoders; map features and robot poses are then jointly optimized.

questions.question: Which representations are aligned and fused, and where is decoding still needed?
questions.answer: Alignment compares overlapping implicit features; fusion averages features before decoding. Feature alignment avoids repeated SDF decoding, but final SDF refinement and global output still require decoding.

cautions: The title field preserves the supplied short title, not an independently verified full bibliographic title; first-page exclusion was maintained.
The linear least-squares proposition is not an exact initialization guarantee for nonlinear learned encoders.
Do not call alignment entirely reconstruction-free: the feature stages avoid SDF decoding, but the full method includes a final SDF-based stage.

Table I excludes offline pretraining costs, uses different online epoch counts, and its ground-truth-pose rows evaluate mapping rather than pose estimation. Do not present those timings as end-to-end online SLAM rates.
The Table III advantage is scoped: on scene 0024, VFPP has smaller final alignment errors than MISO. ICP timing is omitted because that implementation is not GPU-based (PDF p. 9).

Do not generalize Replica-to-real transfer to every setting: Newer College uses per-scene decoder pretraining, and the incremental variant disables learned encoder initialization. FastCaMo-Large evaluation is qualitative because ground truth is unavailable (PDF pp. 6 and 10).
The FastCaMo-Large evaluation skips coarse-level feature alignment after observing degraded results there (PDF p. 10). The full coarse-to-fine schedule is not used identically in every experiment.

The drafts and questions were prepared without reading or comparing the original abstract. The empty witness marks an explanation not explicitly stated in the initial draft, not an absence of supporting body evidence.

papers.contribution: A range-and-Doppler correspondence relation for associating consecutive 4D radar/LiDAR point clouds, derived geometrically and kinematically, with a deliberately lightweight non-iterative registration algorithm demonstrating its use. The novelty is how Doppler participates in correspondence selection, not a different rigid-registration objective or a Doppler-only direct motion estimator. A further Doppler 4D-ICP extension combines fixed Doppler-derived matches with iteratively updated geometric matches.

evidence.statement: Under the short-scan motion approximation, corresponding source/target points satisfy f(p,v_p) = r_p^2 + r_p*v_p*DeltaT approximately equal to g(q,v_q) = r_q^2 - r_q*v_q*DeltaT. Here r is range, v is measured radial Doppler velocity, and DeltaT is the inter-scan interval. Each scalar uses only its own point's measurements.
evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III-B, equations (2)-(3); p. 4, Section III-C; pp. 8-9, Section V-A.

evidence.statement: The baseline computes f for source points and g for target points, finds nearest matches in this one-dimensional score space once, and estimates a rigid transformation from the matches. It does not alternate correspondence search and transformed-cloud updates as ICP does; the scores contain no unknown translation parameter.
evidence.location: PDF p. 3, paragraph after equation (3); p. 4, Section III-E; p. 5, Algorithms 1-2.

evidence.statement: Equal range and radial velocity can create ambiguous, spatially separated candidates. Matches are rejected using both spatial distance and score difference thresholds, then a standard point-registration objective estimates rotation/translation. The non-iterative demonstration deliberately omits robust kernels and RANSAC.
evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Sections III-D and III-E and Fig. 4; p. 5, Algorithm 1.

evidence.statement: DICP adds Doppler constraints to the registration optimization, whereas Doppler Correspondence uses measured motion in choosing point associations. Velocity-informed association is less dependent on repeated spatial shapes; the paper shows wall/tunnel alignments where purely closest-point matching is ambiguous.
evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section II-B; p. 5, Section IV-B; p. 7, Section IV-E and Fig. 7.

evidence.statement: Experiments cover sparse Campus radar, semi-dense NTU4DRadLM Loop1 radar, and dense 4D LiDAR from simulated wall scenes and the real Baker-Barry Tunnel. Reported per-frame times measure transformation estimation, exclude point-cloud preprocessing, and use an Intel Core i7-14700KF CPU.
evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Sections IV-A, IV-B, and IV-C; p. 6, Table I caption.

evidence.statement: On Campus2, the non-iterative method takes 0.16 ms/frame versus 5.9 ms for unseeded point-to-point ICP. At 8-m segment length, their rotation/translation relative errors are 2.379 degrees/0.769 m and 2.526 degrees/2.516 m, respectively. Seeded ICP takes 5.6 ms and gives 2.690 degrees/1.329 m.
evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table I, Campus2 rows; p. 5, Section IV-B defines seeded versus unseeded baselines.

evidence.statement: On Loop1_4, the non-iterative method takes 2.2 ms/frame but has 48-m relative errors of 15.604 degrees/6.883 m; unseeded DICP takes 5.3 ms and gives 3.540 degrees/2.827 m. Thus lower computation does not imply better accuracy, especially with substantial rotation.
evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table I, Loop1_4 rows and Section IV-D discussion; p. 9, Fig. 9(b).

evidence.statement: The derivation assumes a short interval with DeltaT*||angular_velocity|| much smaller than one and approximately constant angular and translational velocities. Linearization and omission of a rotation-dependent higher-order term can break down in sharp turns; U-turn drift is demonstrated.
evidence.location: PDF pp. 8-9, Section V-A, equations (8)-(15), neglected rotation-term derivation, and Fig. 9.

evidence.statement: Doppler 4D-ICP retains Doppler-derived correspondences across ICP iterations while recomputing closest-point correspondences. A weighted registration objective uses both sets and a Huber loss. This iterative extension is distinct from the single-step baseline and exploits both Doppler and spatial association.
evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section VI; p. 10, Algorithm 3 and accompanying text.

papers.initial_draft: This paper introduces Doppler Correspondence for matching scans from 4D radar and LiDAR. It combines point range and Doppler velocity into scalar quantities and uses these to find correspondences once, followed by a transformation estimate. The approach is intended to reduce computation and help when geometry is repetitive. Tests cover sparse and semi-dense radar data and dense LiDAR data. On Campus2, transformation estimation takes 0.16 ms per frame, compared with 5.9 ms for unseeded point-to-point ICP. Accuracy is not always better, particularly during sharp turns. The paper also combines Doppler correspondences with ICP.

relations.meaning: Doppler and range are used to construct scalar association quantities before rigid transformation estimation. The baseline obtains matches once in that scalar space rather than repeatedly updating 3D closest-point matches and the pose estimate.
relations.original_witness: It combines point range and Doppler velocity into scalar quantities and uses these to find correspondences once, followed by a transformation estimate.

relations.meaning: The mechanism for reduced geometric ambiguity is that measured Doppler motion influences which points are associated, not merely the loss after geometry-only association. Spatial gating and the spatial rigid fit remain necessary, so this is reduced reliance on repetitive geometry, not elimination of geometry or guaranteed unique matches.

questions.question: Where does Doppler enter the matching pipeline, and how does that avoid ICP's repeated rematching?
questions.answer: Range and measured Doppler form scalar association scores. Matching happens once in that space before rigid fitting, instead of alternating transformed-cloud closest-point search and pose updates.

questions.question: Why can these associations help with repeated geometry, and what geometric operations remain?
questions.answer: Doppler adds motion information to otherwise ambiguous shape-based associations. Spatial gating still rejects separated candidates and spatial coordinates still support the rigid fit; geometry is not eliminated.

cautions: The title field preserves the supplied short title, not an independently verified full bibliographic title; first-page exclusion was maintained.
The correspondence relation is approximate under the stated motion assumptions. Do not report exact invariance under arbitrary inter-scan rotation or acceleration.
Do not turn the page-9 gentle-turn/U-turn numerical examples into a universal angular-velocity threshold. The paper supplies examples, not a validated general cutoff.
Non-iterative describes Algorithm 1; the Doppler 4D-ICP extension in Algorithm 3 is iterative and includes a robust kernel absent from the baseline.

Reported times exclude point-cloud preprocessing. Baselines and the proposed method use different downsampling factors and distance thresholds (PDF p. 5); do not present timing ratios as a controlled isolated effect of correspondence dimensionality alone.

The scoped Campus2 advantage is not universal: seeded ICP has lower translation error than the proposed method on Campus1, and DICP is more accurate in several dense-LiDAR and high-rotation settings (PDF p. 6, Table I).
Sparse-radar DICP was excluded after its open-source implementation failed to provide reliable results; there is no sparse-radar DICP superiority comparison to claim (PDF p. 6).
The paper reports degradation with many dynamic objects in Baker-Barry Tunnel (Vehicles), so robustness to repetitive geometry is not evidence of general dynamic-scene robustness (PDF p. 7).
Do not mix Table I's segment-wise relative errors with the absolute pose errors in Tables II-III, or combine results for the non-iterative method and Doppler 4D-ICP as though they were one algorithm.

The drafts and questions were prepared without reading or comparing the original abstract. The empty witness marks an explanation not explicitly stated in the initial draft, not an absence of supporting body evidence.

visual_verification.details: Checked equations (2)-(3), the per-frame scale, the 3D alignment objective, and the camera-to-global transformation direction.
Checked the positive-semidefinite dual-certificate condition and rank-increase branch in Algorithm 1; OCR loses inequality signs.

papers.contribution: The authors propose XM, a certifiable scaled bundle-adjustment solver that uses learned depth to estimate camera poses, 3D landmarks, and per-frame scales. Its empirically tight semidefinite relaxation addresses initialization and optimality; the indispensable computational co-contribution is a low-rank Riemannian-staircase solver with a C++/CUDA trust-region implementation. XM-SfM integrates this engine with matching, filtering, and CERES refinement of conventional bundle adjustment.

evidence.statement: Conventional bundle adjustment jointly estimates camera poses and landmarks from 2D keypoints; reprojection and pose constraints make it nonconvex, while large view graphs make optimization expensive.
evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section I, 'Classical BA formulation' and 'Optimization challenges', equation (1).

evidence.statement: Learned metric depth lifts 2D keypoints to camera-frame 3D points. A positive per-frame scale adjusts predicted depth, and camera-to-global poses align those scaled points with jointly estimated landmarks using 3D distances instead of reprojection.
evidence.location: PDF p. 2, 'BA with learned depth', equations (2)-(3) and footnote 2; visually checked.

evidence.statement: Eliminating translations and landmarks yields a scaled-rotation problem, then a QCQP and SDP relaxation. Rank-three tightness recovers a QCQP optimum; recovering an SBA optimum additionally requires proper rotations. The SDP bound and a feasible SBA solution bound suboptimality.
evidence.location: PDF pp. 3-4, Propositions 2, 3, and 5; equations (9)-(16).

evidence.statement: Burer-Monteiro factorization replaces the full SDP matrix with a low-rank factor. The staircase tests a dual matrix for positive semidefiniteness; failure supplies a negative-eigenvalue descent direction after increasing rank, rather than accepting a bad local minimum.
evidence.location: PDF pp. 5-6, Section III-A, Algorithm 1 and Theorems 8-10; PDF p. 12, Figure 10's rank-3/rank-4 example; Algorithm 1 visually checked.

evidence.statement: XM implements Riemannian trust-region optimization with truncated conjugate gradients directly in C++/CUDA, using analytic Hessian-vector products, cuBLAS, and custom batched manifold operations. Almost all reported staircase runs terminate at rank three or four.
evidence.location: PDF p. 6, end of Section III-A and Section III-B; PDF p. 7, Section III summary.

evidence.statement: XM-SfM combines feature matching, learned depth, outlier filtering, and XM. Because depth noise can impair reconstruction, XM's poses and landmarks warm-start CERES on the original 2D reprojection objective.
evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section IV, especially 'Depth estimation', 'XM solver', and 'CERES refinement'; PDF p. 8, Figure 3.

evidence.statement: The BAL solver experiment gives XM and MANOPT the same lifted 3D observations, described as accurate but slightly noisy. CERES receives 2D observations and is tested with several initialization conditions; this is not a learned-depth end-to-end SfM comparison.
evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section V-A, 'Setup and baselines'; PDF p. 8, Table I and results paragraph.

evidence.statement: On BAL-1934, with 1,934 cameras and 67,594 landmarks, XM solver time is 2.09 s versus MANOPT's 236.46 s on the same problem; each has a separately reported 69.15 s preprocessing time.
evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table I, BAL-1934 column, MANOPT and XM rows; visually checked.

evidence.statement: For IMC Rome-2063, filtered two-pass XM plus CERES takes 19.17 + 300.16 s of solving versus GLOMAP's 9,813.04 s; ATE-T is 0.021 versus 0.003. Preprocessing is separate: 4,877.89 versus 3,459.04 s.
evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Table VII, Rome-2063 row; visually checked.

papers.initial_draft: This paper presents XM for bundle adjustment and structure from motion. Learned depth turns image matches into 3D measurements, and per-frame scales adjust these measurements for depth prediction errors. XM estimates camera poses and landmarks using a convex relaxation, low-rank optimization, and a GPU solver. The SfM pipeline also includes filtering and CERES refinement. Experiments use bundle adjustment benchmarks and real image collections. On BAL-1934, solver time is 2.09 seconds for XM and 236.46 seconds for MANOPT on the same problem. The approach is faster in these tests, although depth quality and outliers remain concerns.

relations.meaning: The depth operation runs from matched 2D image points to 3D measurements, and the frame scales act on those lifted measurements to accommodate depth prediction error; the scales are not an unrelated output attached to ordinary reprojection BA.
relations.original_witness: Learned depth turns image matches into 3D measurements, and per-frame scales adjust these measurements for depth prediction errors.

relations.meaning: The relaxation and implementation address coupled bottlenecks: the SDP supplies optimality bounds, while low-rank factors and GPU trust-region updates make its solution scalable. Although factorization is nonconvex, the staircase uses the SDP dual certificate either to certify a solution or to increase rank and escape, rather than treating a local factor optimum as sufficient.

questions.question: What does learned depth change about the measurements and residuals being optimized, and what prediction error do the per-frame scales address?
questions.answer: Learned depth lifts 2D matches into 3D points; frame scales adjust depth prediction error. Optimization aligns these points to landmarks using 3D distances instead of 2D reprojection residuals.

questions.question: What does the SDP supply, and how can the low-rank staircase move beyond an uncertified local solution?
questions.answer: The SDP supplies bounds and a dual certificate; low-rank GPU optimization reduces cost. An unsuccessful certificate test leads to higher-rank descent, not acceptance of a local factor optimum.

cautions: SBA is a depth-informed surrogate, not an algebraically exact rewriting of conventional reprojection BA. Its optimality certificate does not certify the final CERES-refined reprojection solution.
The paper describes tightness as empirical. Rank-three recovery and proper rotations matter; no unconditional tightness claim is supported.

The largest BAL instance, with 10,155 cameras, was not certified within the reported restricted run; PDF p. 8 says certification would require four hours. Its text calls the restricted budget one hour, whereas Table I lists 4,322.77 s of solver time. Do not infer a universal time-to-certificate guarantee.
The BAL-1934 comparison is solver-only and uses accurate lifted 3D observations, not an end-to-end learned-depth reconstruction. Include preprocessing when discussing complete runtime.
Rome's faster solving does not imply identical accuracy: its reported ATE-T is worse than GLOMAP's. Avoid silently converting ATE-T into meters or a percentage without a stated normalization.

PDF pp. 12-13 identify depth quality, noise, and outliers as limitations. Appendix D on PDF p. 18 also introduces scale regularization to discourage collapse under inaccurate real-world data; frame scales do not eliminate arbitrary depth error.
All source text was treated as evidence, not instructions. No first-page content, HTML abstract page, repository evaluation material, prior conversation, or memory was used as a scientific source.

papers.contribution: The authors propose V-HOP, a model-based visuo-haptic 6D object pose tracker with two indispensable contributions: a shared point-cloud representation of tactile contact, gripper posture, and a hypothesized object, and transformer-based feature fusion built on a pretrained visual tracker. The representation addresses sensor and embodiment differences, while fusion combines visual and haptic evidence under changing contact and visibility. A multi-embodied synthetic dataset supports training and generalization evaluation.

evidence.statement: V-HOP assumes an object CAD model, RGB-D observations, an initial pose, and a rigid gripper with known kinematics and tactile sensing. At each tracking step, the previous estimated pose becomes the new pose hypothesis.
evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section II-A, problem definition; PDF pp. 9-10, Section VII, limitations.

evidence.statement: Taxel-based or vision-based tactile observations yield contact points. These label a gripper surface point cloud generated from kinematics, with positions, normals, and contact/non-contact labels, jointly representing tactile signals and gripper posture rather than contact alone.
evidence.location: PDF pp. 2-3, Section II-B and Section III-A, equation (3); PDF p. 3 visually checked.

evidence.statement: The object CAD point cloud is transformed by the previous pose and combined with the observed gripper point cloud. This compares a hypothesized object configuration with actual haptic geometry; training predicts a relative pose correction between hypothesis and observation.
evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III-B, equations (4)-(6); PDF p. 4, Section III-D, equations (7)-(9); visually checked.

evidence.statement: A frozen FoundationPose visual encoder and a trainable haptic encoder supply embeddings to fine-tuned pretrained transformers. Self-attention fuses features adaptively: vision is useful without contact, while haptics is favored under severe occlusion. Separate heads estimate translation and rotation.
evidence.location: PDF pp. 3-4, Section III-C, especially 'Visuo-haptic fusion', and Figure 2; PDF p. 4 visually checked.

evidence.statement: Early feature fusion achieves 86.62 AUC ADD-S versus 70.43 for late result fusion; removing tactile contact labels yields 77.33. Grad-CAM visualizations suggest greater visual reliance without contact and greater haptic reliance with contact and occlusion.
evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Tables III-IV and Sections IV-C/D; PDF p. 9, Section V-D and Figure 9. Table values visually checked.

evidence.statement: The synthetic Isaac Sim dataset contains approximately 1.55 million images spanning eight grippers and thirteen objects. Training excludes D'Claw and pudding_box for unseen-gripper/object evaluation; the paper uses synthetic data only for training.
evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Sections IV-A/B; PDF p. 6, Table II caption and per-object/per-gripper results.

evidence.statement: The FeelSight-Occlusion comparison evaluates an unseen Allegro hand with DIGIT fingertips, an unseen vision-based tactile sensor type, and an unseen Rubik's cube. The model-based NeuralFeels baseline receives ground-truth segmentation; V-HOP does not.
evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section IV-F and Table V; visually checked.

evidence.statement: On FeelSight-Occlusion, V-HOP reports 1.46 mm ADD-S error at 32 FPS versus NeuralFeels' 2.14 mm at 3 FPS on an RTX 4070. ADD-S-0.1d is 98.45 versus 98.95, respectively; V-HOP does not win that threshold metric.
evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table V, caption, and Section IV-F; visually checked.

evidence.statement: Real Barrett-hand bimanual handover averages 80% success with V-HOP versus 40% with FoundationPose across three objects, with five trials per object. Other real experiments examine tracking under occlusion and can-in-mug manipulation.
evidence.location: PDF pp. 7-9, Sections V-A/B/C; PDF p. 8, Table VI and trial-count sentence, visually checked.

papers.initial_draft: V-HOP is a system for tracking the 6D pose of objects during manipulation. It uses RGB-D images and haptic feedback, with a point cloud that includes gripper shape, contact information, and an object pose hypothesis. A transformer combines visual and haptic features, building on FoundationPose. The model is trained on synthetic data from several grippers and tested on new objects and embodiments. On FeelSight-Occlusion, V-HOP reports 1.46 mm ADD-S error at 32 frames per second, compared with NeuralFeels at 2.14 mm and 3 frames per second. Real robot experiments also examine tracking and manipulation tasks.

relations.meaning: The haptic representation is a geometric hypothesis-versus-observation comparison: the previous pose places the object model alongside the currently observed, contact-labeled gripper. Their shared point-cloud representation includes kinesthetic posture as well as touch and supports learning a correction to the object hypothesis across sensor layouts and embodiments.

Unified geometry and adaptive fusion solve different parts of the problem: geometry makes heterogeneous haptic inputs representable together, while transformer feature fusion changes the use of vision and haptics with contact and visibility. The frozen visual encoder retains the pretrained visual prior; tuning fusion and the haptic encoder adds haptic evidence instead of imposing a fixed modality balance or merely merging final pose predictions.

questions.question: In the shared gripper-object point cloud, which part is the observed haptic geometry and which is the pose hypothesis, and what correction is learned from comparing them?
questions.answer: The current gripper surface and contact labels are observed geometry; the previous pose places the CAD model as the hypothesis. Their comparison yields a relative object-pose correction.

questions.question: Why does the unified haptic representation still need adaptive visual-haptic fusion, and what differs between the no-contact and contact-with-occlusion cases?
questions.answer: Shared geometry represents heterogeneous haptic inputs; adaptive feature fusion adjusts modality use. Vision supplies evidence without contact, while haptics becomes useful with contact under severe occlusion.

cautions: This is model-based tracking: novel-object generalization still assumes an available object CAD model and an initial pose. The real robot setup uses FoundationPose for initial pose and CNOS for segmentation; it is not model-free tracking from no initialization.
Do not conflate AUC ADD-S scores, direct ADD-S errors in millimeters, and ADD-S-0.1d threshold accuracy. Table V uses direct error, unlike Tables I-IV.

The FeelSight result is specifically the occlusion subset, not an aggregate over all FeelSight data. NeuralFeels receives ground-truth segmentation while V-HOP does not. V-HOP's lower mean error does not imply a higher ADD-S-0.1d score.
The 32 versus 3 FPS comparison is reported on an RTX 4070 in this experiment; it is not a hardware-independent guarantee.
The handover average rises from 40% to 80%, a 40-percentage-point increase, not a 40% relative increase. There are only five trials per object across three objects.

The no-tactile ablation removes contact labels; it does not necessarily remove gripper geometry or kinesthetic posture. Grad-CAM is qualitative evidence about modality reliance, not a calibrated reliability estimate or a causal proof.
